The commercial, instrument-rated pilot was departing under special visual flight rules clearance in instrument meteorological conditions. Shortly after takeoff the pilot encountered a dense fog bank while flying over the calm water of a river. He stated he attempted to turn around, but he lost his visual reference with the river. The pilot stated he then attempted to climb but became disoriented and a few seconds later the helicopter impacted the water. 
Examination of the airframe and engine revealed no evidence of any preaccident mechanical failures or malfunctions that would have precluded normal operation.
20240907195072.fa:
HISTORY OF FLIGHTOn September 7, 2024, about 0924 Alaska daylight time, a Bell 206B helicopter, N306FW, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near King Salmon, Alaska. A passenger was fatally injured; the pilot and three passengers sustained minor injuries. The helicopter was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 135 flight.
The accident helicopter, owned and operated by Egli Air Haul, was transporting four passengers to a sport fishing camp located to the south of the King Salmon Airport (AKN). According to archived FAA data, the accident pilot contacted the AKN control tower specialist on duty to request a special visual flight rules (SVFR) clearance to depart to the south. The controller on duty issued the pilot a SVFR clearance and instructed the pilot to report clear of the Class D airspace to the south. The helicopter then departed to the south. 
Shortly after the helicopter departed, the control tower specialist received a phone call from an observer to the south of the airport indicating that a helicopter had just crashed into the Naknak River, near Grassy Point. The control tower specialist then attempted to reach the departing helicopter, but no further radio communications were received.
The pilot reported encountering a very dense fog bank while flying over the calm water of the Naknek River; he subsequently lost all visual reference and became disoriented when he attempted to climb. The helicopter then descended and subsequently impacted the surface of the river. 
Witnesses reported that it was foggy at the airport before the helicopter departed. One witness, who was walking along the riverbank, reported that it was so foggy that she could not see the opposite side of the river. This witness saw the helicopter just before the impact and stated it was flying less the 100 ft above the water. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATIONThe fuselage was intact with all major components still attached. The tail rotor blades, and gear box were undamaged. Cyclic and collective flight controls were traced from the cockpit controls to the pitch control rods attached to the main rotor hub assembly. Anti-torque control (yaw) was traced from the anti-torque pedals to the tail rotor with fractures consistent with impact damage at the bottom and top of the flight control “broom closet.” Tail rotor pitch control operated smoothly and freely. No damage was observed with the flight control hydraulic servos. All hoses were attached and undamaged. All fuel, oil, and electrical lines in the engine compartment were undamaged and connected. The fuel control unit was undamaged. Throttle control from the cockpit was traced to the fuel control unit. Rotational scoring was observed on the tail rotor drive shaft under the engine and on the input shaft to the K-flex. SURVIVAL ASPECTSThe passenger who was fatally injured was unable to exit the helicopter when the helicopter went under the water. The passenger was in the front left seat using a 4-point seatbelt restraint system.

The pilot of the helicopter reported that while repositioning closer to the loading equipment, the helicopter experienced collective bounce. He attempted to maneuver the helicopter to avoid equipment and personnel; however, control was lost and the helicopter impacted terrain. 
The operator reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures that would have precluded normal operations. The operators manual for the helicopter stated, in part, “Collective bounce is a pilot Induced vertical oscillation of the collective control system when an absolute friction (either pilot applied, or control rigged) is less than seven pounds. It may be encountered in any flight condition by a rapid buildup of vertical bounce at approximately three cycles per second. The seventy of the oscillation is such that effective control of the helicopter may become difficult to maintain. The pilot should apply and maintain adequate collective friction in all flight conditions.”

20240910195092.an: As Delta Air Lines flight 295 (DAL295) was taxiing behind Endeavor Air dba Delta Connection flight 5526 (EDV5526), the right wingtip of DAL295 impacted the vertical stabilizer of EDV5526 at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL), Atlanta, Georgia, resulting in separation of the vertical stabilizer. EDV5526 was holding short of runway 8R on taxiway H waiting for a takeoff clearance as DAL295 was taxiing on taxiway E to hold short of taxiway V. EDV5526 stopped about 56 ft from the hold short line, resulting in insufficient clearance for an A350 to pass behind it on taxiway E. At the time of the collision, the captain of DAL295 was focused on ensuring the airplane’s left wingtip would not impinge on traffic exiting taxiway V while the first officer (FO) of DAL295 was locating taxiway V on the navigation display and electronic flight bag (EFB). As a result, neither the captain nor the FO of DAL295 identified the loss of clearance between their right wingtip and the empennage of EDV5526.
20240910195092.fa:
On September 10, 2024, about 1007 eastern daylight time (EDT), DAL295, an Airbus A350-941, N503DN, collided with EDV5526, a Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (MHI) RJ CL-600-2D24 (CRJ-900), N302PQ, while taxiing for departure at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL), Atlanta, Georgia. The 15 crewmembers and 221 passengers on board DAL295 were uninjured. Three crewmembers and 56 passengers on board EDV5526 were uninjured and one crewmember sustained minor injuries. 
DAL295 was a scheduled international passenger flight operating under the provisions of Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 121 from ATL to Haneda Airport (HND), Tokyo, Japan. EDV5526 was a scheduled domestic passenger flight operating under the provisions of Title 14 CFR Part 121 from ATL to Lafayette Regional Airport (LFT), Lafayette, Louisiana. EDV5526 was holding short of runway 8R on taxiway H waiting for a takeoff clearance. As DAL295 passed behind EDV5526 on taxiway E, its right wingtip impacted the vertical stabilizer of EDV5526, resulting in substantial damage to the CRJ-900 and minor damage to the A350 (see figure 1).

Figure 1. The damaged empennage of EDV5526. (Source: Atlanta Department of Aviation)
At the time of the accident, runway 9L was normally used for larger aircraft but was closed for construction. Therefore, DAL295 was scheduled to depart from runway 8R. After pushback from the gate, the flight crew of DAL295 received taxi instructions to proceed north on taxiway D and hold short of taxiway G. DAL295 taxied as instructed and received further instructions to taxi on taxiway G and to hold short of taxiway F.
They were subsequently cleared to taxi on taxiway F and to transition to taxiway E. After DAL295 turned onto taxiway E, ground control instructed the flight crew to have the airplane follow EDV5526 on taxiway E and to switch to the airport traffic control tower’s (ATCT) frequency. As DAL295 continued to taxi on taxiway E, the flight crew observed a navigational alert message, "NAV GNSS-2,” on the lower electronic centralized aircraft monitor (ECAM). The first officer (FO) informed the tower that they would need to stop to coordinate with maintenance before departure. ATC instructed the flight crew to continue straight ahead on taxiway E and to hold short of taxiway V to troubleshoot the problem (see figure 2).

Figure 2. Ground position tracks for DAL295 and EDV5526 in relation to taxiways E and H. The white circle denotes the location of the collision. In this image, both airplanes were traveling from the right to the left on taxiway E.
The captain of DAL295 recalled that, as the airplane approached the intersection with taxiway V, he was focused on ensuring the left wingtip was not impinging on traffic that was coming off of taxiway V. The FO of DAL295 stated he was looking at the navigation display’s Airport Navigation Function and his EFB to identify taxiway V, and was querying the captain about taxiway V. 
Around that time, the right wingtip of DAL295 impacted the vertical stabilizer of EDV5526, which was holding short of runway 8R at taxiway H. Following the collision, the captain of DAL295 stopped the airplane and set the parking brake. After airport rescue and firefighting (ARFF) examined the exterior of the airplane, the flight crew of DAL295 was given clearance to return to the gate.
The flight crew of EDV5526 stated they pushed back from the gate and that ground control instructed them to taxi to runway 8R via taxiway E. The flight crew completed the “before takeoff” checks while on taxiway E, and ATC advised the crew that DAL295 would wait for them and to monitor the ATCT’s frequency for takeoff. The captain stated she maneuvered the airplane to the hold short line on taxiway H, set the parking brake, and awaited further instruction from ATC (see figure 3).
 
Figure 3. Ground position tracks of DAL295 and EDV5526 leading up to the collision.
Based on the distance of the nose landing gear of EDV5526 to the hold short line on taxiway H, EDV5526 was about 56 ft from the hold short line (see figure 4). The wingtip distance of DAL295 was estimated to be about 106 ft from the centerline of taxiway E. 

Figure 4. The estimated distance of EDV5526 from the hold short line on taxiway H and the estimated distance of the wingtip of DAL295 from the centerline of taxiway E. 

Crew Information
DAL295 Flight Crew
The captain was hired by Delta Air Lines on November 8, 1990, and received his initial type rating on the A350 on January 20, 2023. 
The FO was hired by Delta Air Lines on November 1, 1996, and received his initial type rating on the A350 on May 20, 2018. 
EDV5526 Flight Crew
The captain was hired by Endeavor Air on September 3, 2019, and received her initial type rating for the CRJ-900 on November 12, 2019.
The FO was hired by Endeavor Air on April 17, 2023, and received his initial type rating for the CRJ-900 on June 30, 2023.
Damage to Aircraft
The empennage of the CRJ-900 remained attached to the fuselage by the flight control cables, electrical wiring, and a small section of vertical stabilizer skin. The left side of the aft fuselage exhibited dents and deformation above and below the pylon structure. The right side of the aft fuselage showed two areas of tensile deformation resulting in imprinting of the underlying frames on the skin.
Damage to the right wing of the A350 was limited to the outboard section, starting near the outboard end of the outboard slat and continuing up to the winglet. Blue paint transfer and scrape damage was observed in the outboard section of the right wing. 

Flight Recorders
The cockpit voice recorder (CVR) and flight data recorder (FDR) from both airplanes were downloaded and analyzed in conjunction with Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) data. The estimated time of collision between the two airplanes was at 1007:46 EDT. EDV5526 was stationary and DAL295 was taxiing at a groundspeed of about 12 knots. EDV5526 sustained lateral accelerations of 0.5 gravitational force equivalent (g) left followed by 0.55g right, and its heading had rotated about 9° clockwise. 
The flight crew of DAL295 exclaimed surprise when the collision occurred and was not aware of what they collided with. After the collision, the flight crew of DAL295 stated they were on the centerline of the taxiway and that they were following their taxi instructions. Immediately after the collision, the captain of EDV5526 stated they thought another aircraft had collided with them and later commented that they “can’t pull forward anymore” in reference to their location to the hold short line.
Additional Information
The visibility of the A350 wingtips from the captain and FO seats was assessed by investigators. This assessment determined that the pilots would have to get out of their seats in order to see the wingtips from the cockpit’s aft-most windows. Due to parallax of looking aft and slight distortion from the thick glass of the window, the assessment determined that it would be difficult to assess if the wingtip had adequate clearance to a nearby airplane if a crewmember were to look out of the aft-most window.

Safety Actions
After this accident, Delta Air Lines published a reminder to crews in an internal newsletter about remaining vigilant during ground operations, particularly in identifying new threats as they may appear. Delta also added information in the flight operations manual regarding areas of vulnerability during ground operations, to include individual crewmembers announcing when they are “heads down” to perform certain tasks that reduce their ability to monitor outside the cockpit.

20240911195102.an:
While performing touch-and-go landings, the flight instructor and student pilot noticed a partial loss of engine power on climbout, about 200 ft above ground level (agl). The flight instructor reported the tachometer read 2,100 and then 1,600 rpm. During a forced landing to a golf course, the airplane’s nose landing gear collapsed and the airplane came to rest inverted.
A postimpact test of the engine’s fuel injection servo found fuel flow below the minimum service limit at most test points. When the servo was disassembled, a thick blue liquid consistent with a fuel-oil mixture was found in the venturi chambers. Oil residue was noted in the hex plug and air diaphragm, the spring and stem assembly, and the air passage to the air diaphragm. No other anomalies were detected with the engine.
A service bulletin from the fuel injection servo manufacturer states that this type of contamination could cause an engine to exhibit “gradually deteriorating idle, difficulty starting and/or cold engine acceleration performance.” The flight school was aware of the service bulletin and was inspecting airplanes that had the engine symptoms listed in the service bulletin. 
It is likely that contamination of the fuel injection servo resulted in a partial loss of engine power and subsequent forced landing.
20240911195102.fa:
On September 11, 2024, about 0940 mountain daylight time, a Cessna 172S airplane, N20747, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Englewood, Colorado. The flight instructor was not injured and the student pilot sustained minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight.
The pilots were performing touch-and-go landings on runway 17R at Centennial Airport (APA), Englewood, Colorado. On climbout for the traffic pattern, when the airplane was about 200 ft agl, the pilots noticed a partial loss of engine power. The instructor reported the tachometer read 2,100 and then 1,600 rpm. He performed a forced landing to a golf course. During the landing roll, the airplane’s nose landing gear collapsed and the airplane came to rest inverted.
A review of maintenance logbook entries found that on September 5, 2024, about one week before the accident flight, another pilot reported that the airplane “was only getting 2,000 rpm at max power and was backfiring constantly in the run-up.” However, maintenance personnel found that the engine operated satisfactorily during a subsequent ground run-up. The airplane was then flown daily without any reported engine problems until the accident takeoff.
A postimpact examination of the engine revealed no evidence of any preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures that would have precluded normal operation. However, during a bench test of the engine’s fuel injection servo (AVStar part number LFR-NNSS5), fuel flow was below the minimum service limit at most test points. When the servo was disassembled, a thick blue liquid consistent with a fuel-oil mixture was found in the venturi chambers. Oil residue was noted in the hex plug and air diaphragm, the spring and stem assembly, and the air passage to the air diaphragm. 
The AVStar LFR-NNSS5 is a variant of the RSA-5AD1 fuel injection servo and was mounted in an updraft configuration on the accident airplane. AVStar service bulletin AFS-SB10, Fuel Servos Installed in an Updraft Configuration, is applicable to RSA-5AD1 servos and states:
There have been occasional reports of servo equipped engines that exhibit one or more of the following characteristics - gradually deteriorating idle, difficulty starting and/or cold engine acceleration performance. These engines may have the servo mounted in an updraft, or nearly updraft configuration. Close inspection of the servo may reveal oily contaminant in the bore of the servo that is green/blue in color. It is also possible for this contaminant to migrate into the air section of the regulator.
The Precision Airmotive service information letter SIL RS-40, Service Information For RSA-5 Series Fuel Injection Servos Installed in Updraft Configuration, similarly notes reports of reduced engine performance and recommends inspection of fuel injection servos for contamination if these problems are experienced. 
The flight school’s maintenance personnel stated they were aware of AVStar AFS-SB10 and Precision Airmotive SIL ARS-40 and routinely inspected their airplanes that had any symptoms listed in AFS-SB10. In addition, they reported that they caution their pilots against over-priming the engine during engine starts.

20240911195105.an: The pilot of the amphibious airplane reported that during the approach to a lake over glassy water, he misjudged the height of the airplane above the water’s surface. He reported that he “had no sense of depth perception” and the airplane impacted the water when he thought it was about 10 ft above the surface. The pilot chose to set the airplane on the water surface to avoid departing with possible damage. However, the airplane handed hard and the float struts collapsed, which resulted in substantial damage to the fuselage. The pilot reported there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.

The pilot was conducting a personal flight when during cruise descent the engine began to sputter and suddenly lost power. He moved the throttle to full-forward and increased the mixture to full-rich, but the engine resumed operation only 5 to 10 seconds before it lost power a second time. The pilot reported that the airplane was at low altitude that required an immediate forced landing into a nearby cornfield. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the engine mounts, fuselage structure, and right wing.

Examination of the airplane fuel system and the engine revealed no evidence of a preimpact mechanical malfunction. There was ample fuel recovered from the fuel tanks at the accident site, and there was no evidence of any water or particulate contamination of the fuel system.

The weather conditions at the time of the accident were in the range of susceptibility for the formation of serious carburetor icing at glide engine power. According to a Federal Aviation Administration Special Airworthiness Information Bulletin, pilots should use carburetor heat while in weather conditions where carburetor icing is probable. When interviewed, the pilot acknowledged that he did not review a carburetor icing chart before the flight. However, he stipulated that he applied carburetor heat after the engine began sputtering.

Based on the available information, the loss of engine power was likely due to carburetor ice accumulation. Additionally, the low altitude at which the loss of engine power occurred significantly reduced the amount of time available to the pilot to troubleshoot and restore engine power before the forced landing.
20240913195116.fa:
On September 12, 2024, about 1205 central daylight time, a Piper PA-12 airplane, N7878M, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Cumberland, Wisconsin. The pilot was not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.

The pilot reported that the airplane was established in cruise flight at 2,100 ft mean sea level with the throttle set about 2,300 rpm and the mixture leaned to rich-of-peak when he entered a descent toward Cumberland Municipal Airport (CBE), Cumberland, Wisconsin. The pilot stated that he did not make any throttle or mixture control changes when he began his descent, and that the engine was using fuel from both wing fuel tanks.

The pilot reported that about 5 miles from CBE, while in cruise descent the engine began to sputter and then suddenly lost power. He moved the throttle to full-forward and increased the mixture to full-rich, but the engine resumed operation only 5 to 10 seconds before it lost power a second time.

The pilot reported the airplane was at a low altitude that required an immediate forced landing into a nearby cornfield. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the engine mounts, fuselage structure, and right wing.

Examination of the airplane fuel system and the engine revealed no evidence of a preimpact mechanical malfunction. There was ample fuel recovered from the fuel tanks at the accident site, and there was no evidence of any water or particulate contamination of the fuel system.

Internal engine and valve train continuity were confirmed as the crankshaft was rotated through the propeller flange. Compression and suction were noted on all four cylinders in conjunction with crankshaft rotation. A lighted borescope inspection of each cylinder did not reveal any anomalies with the cylinders, pistons, valves, valve seats. Both magnetos remained attached to their engine installation points and produced spark at each ignition lead. The upper spark plugs exhibited features consistent with normal engine operation. The engine oil sump contained ample oil, and the disassembled oil filter did not reveal any evidence of contamination. The carburetor fuel inlet screen exhibited no evidence of contamination.

The throttle cable was broken at the clevis, but the carburetor throttle position remained in a wide-open position. The mixture control was found in the full-rich position, and the full-rich mechanical stop-pin was found fractured.

The cockpit carburetor heat control was found turned off. Cable continuity was confirmed from the carburetor heat control to the airbox control; however, due to impact-related damage to the airbox, the carburetor heat valve could not move. A borescope was inserted into the damaged airbox and did not reveal any evidence of rubbing/scratching between the carburetor heat valve and the airbox.

According to a carburetor icing probability chart contained in Federal Aviation Administration Special Airworthiness Information Bulletin CE-09-35, Carburetor Icing Prevention, the recorded temperature and dew point at the time of the accident were in the range of susceptibility for the formation of serious carburetor icing at glide engine power. According to the bulletin, if ice forms in the carburetor of a fixed-pitch propeller aircraft, the restriction to the induction airflow will result in decreased power output and a drop in engine rpm, which might be accompanied or followed by a rough running engine. The bulletin also notes that a pilot should respond to carburetor icing by applying full carburetor heat immediately and that the engine may run rough initially for a short time while the ice melts. The bulletin further recommends that a pilot use carburetor heat when operating the engine at low power settings or while in weather conditions in which carburetor icing is probable.

When interviewed, the pilot acknowledged that he did not review a carburetor icing chart before the flight. However, he stipulated that he applied carburetor heat after the engine began sputtering.

The pilot estimated that he touched down about 100 ft past the numbers while landing. He attempted to decelerate, keeping constant pressure on the brakes. The pilot stated that the brakes were not working until he approached the end of the runway, at which point the brakes “slowly got responsive.” The pilot reported that a go-around was possible and that it was a “shock” that he couldn’t stop the airplane. He reported that the approach and landing was made with the flaps set to “APP.”
The airplane exited the paved surface of the runway and impacted a runway end identifier light, resulting in substantial damage to the fuselage.
A postaccident examination of the brake system revealed no anomalies that would have precluded normal operation, and a postaccident runway inspection by the airport manager revealed visible tire skid marks leading off the end of the runway.
An aircraft performance study using ADS-B and engine control unit (ECU) data concluded that the airplane touched down at 92 kts calibrated airspeed (KCAS), 6 kts faster than the 86-kt VREF speed calculated from the airplane flight manual. The airplane’s weight on wheels sensors indicated that the airplane was not fully on the ground until 2,136 ft past the runway threshold. The airplane landed in a 6.3 kt tailwind that would have increased landing distance by 21%. Considering all factors, the study concluded that insufficient runway remained after the touchdown for the airplane to stop. Additionally, the study concluded that had the pilot used the LDG flap setting, there would have been sufficient runway remaining.
20240913195117.fa:
On September 1, 2024, about 1520 central daylight time, a Diamond DA42 airplane, N705JP, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Mandan, North Dakota. The pilot and passenger were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
According to the pilot, he departed Bismark Municipal Airport (BIS) and requested vectors for the RNAV 31 approach at Mandan Regional Airport (Y19) from air traffic control. The pilot reported that his approach to Y19 was uneventful and estimated that he touched down about 100 ft past the numbers for runway 31. The pilot attempted to decelerate, keeping constant pressure on the brakes. The pilot stated that the brakes were not working until he approached the end of the runway, at which point the brakes “slowly got responsive.” The pilot stated that the pilot-rated passenger asked about conducting a go-around during the landing attempt, but the pilot was focused on stopping. The pilot reported that a go-around could have been possible and that it was a “shock” that he couldn’t stop the airplane. According to the pilot, he used a flap setting of 20°, or APP during the approach and landing.
According to the pilot-rated passenger, the landing at Y19 was so smooth that he did not notice the airplane had touched down until the nose wheel shimmied. The passenger stated that the airplane appeared to touchdown within the first third of the 4399-ft runway and the landing roll seemed normal, but he did not feel as much deceleration as he expected.
The airplane exited the paved surface of the runway and impacted a runway end identifier light, resulting in substantial damage to the fuselage.
According to the airport manager, who examined the runway surface after the accident, there were visible tire skid marks leading off the end of the runway.
A postaccident examination of the brake system revealed that the brakes appeared to function normally. There was no evidence of leaks at the hoses, calipers, or at the master cylinders attached to the rudder pedals. Brake application was firm and, with the brakes applied, would have prevented the movement of the airplane. The brake pads appeared to have adequate material left to not impede braking action. The right brake pads were worn more than the left, but not beyond the limit of function.
An aircraft performance study using ADS-B and engine ECU data concluded that the airplane touched down at 92 kts calibrated airspeed, 6 kts faster than the 86-kt VREF speed calculated from the Airplane Flight Manual. The airplane’s weight on wheels (WOW) sensors indicated that the airplane was not fully on the ground until 2,136 ft past the runway threshold. The airplane was landed in a 6.3-kt tailwind that would have increased landing distance by 21%. Considering all factors, the study concluded that there was insufficient runway remaining after the touchdown for the airplane to stop. Additionally, the study concluded that had the pilot used the LDG flap setting there would have been sufficient runway remaining.
According to the AFM, ground roll distances for flaps LDG are about 73% of the ground roll distances for flaps APP/UP. If that ratio holds for the ground roll estimate above of 2,411 ft with flaps APP, the ground roll estimate for flaps LDG would be 1,760 ft. A ground roll of 1,760 ft would have allowed the airplane to stop on the runway.

The pilot had flown the airplane on two separate uneventful flights earlier that day and was departing on another flight around the airport traffic pattern with two passengers when the engine lost power during takeoff. The pilot landed fast on the remaining portion of the runway. With the throttle still applied, engine power resumed, causing the airplane to become airborne again. The engine then lost power again when the airplane was beyond the departure end of the runway, causing the pilot to land on grass. The airplane then rolled along terrain before coming to rest adjacent to a building on the airport property, with substantial damage to the airplane’s right wing.

Postaccident examination of the engine, engine controls including carburetor heat, fuel supply, fuel vent, air induction, exhaust, and ignition systems revealed no evidence of preimpact failure or malfunction that would have precluded normal operation. Although operational testing of the carburetor revealed no discrepancies with the accelerator pump, mixture control, or performance of the main circuit, subsequent testing revealed restriction of the float caused by the float pontoons contacting the interior walls of the test bowl. Further, the float hinge was worn 0.002 inches beyond specified limits.

Although the carburetor had been in service for more than 43 years, it was considered an on-condition item for Part 91 operators and, as such, was not subject to a set overhaul period based on calendar or operational time. Based on the results of the postaccident examination, the carburetor’s undetected worn internal parts likely restricted movement of the float, preventing fuel from entering the float bowl as fuel was consumed during takeoff, which resulted in fuel starvation. Additionally, had the pilot reduced throttle when performing the first forced landing on the remaining portion of the runway, the flight duration would have been shortened, lessening the chance for airplane damage.
20240916195125.fa:
On September 14, 2024, about 1405 eastern daylight time, a Piper PA-32-260 airplane, N6FT, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Baltimore, Maryland. The commercial pilot and two passengers were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.

The pilot stated that earlier that day he had flown the airplane on two uneventful flights. The accident flight was intended to fly two passengers around the airport traffic pattern for about 10 minutes. After starting the engine, he taxied the airplane to runway 15L and waited about 10 to 15 minutes while in line to depart. After being cleared for takeoff, with the fuel selector positioned to the left main fuel tank and the auxiliary fuel pump on, he applied full power and the engine responded. He rotated at 80 mph halfway down the 5,000-ft-long runway. He reported the takeoff roll distance was a little longer than normal, but he attributed that to the ambient temperature (about 82° F) and because the airplane was a little heavier than normal. He accelerated to between 110 and 115 mph, but when the airplane was about 200 ft above the runway, the engine lost total power. He pushed the elevator control forward and touched down far along the runway at a fast airspeed. He reported that he believed the throttle was still fully forward. The engine regained power and the airplane rotated again and continued past the end of the runway before the engine stopped again. He then pushed the elevator forward and touched down on grass on airport property, avoiding obstacles, before the airplane crested a hill and then came to rest adjacent to a building on airport property.

Examination of the airplane at the accident site by an FAA inspector revealed the right wing was substantially damaged and the right main fuel tank was breached, but the left was not. No contaminants were noted in the left main fuel tank.

Examination of the engine by an FAA airworthiness inspector revealed no evidence of preimpact failure or malfunction of the engine, engine controls including carburetor heat, fuel supply, fuel vent, air induction, exhaust, or ignition system including the magnetos, which tested satisfactory. Although the FAA inspector reported he was unable to remove the carburetor bowl drain plug, the carburetor bowl was later examined and did not contain any fuel, but some black specs exited the inlet opening. The carburetor was retained for further examination.

Operational testing of the carburetor with NTSB oversight revealed no anomalies to the accelerator pump, mixture control, or performance of the main circuit. Disassembly of the carburetor revealed no abrasions on the interior of the float bowl from the brown foam-type float. Installation of a cutaway test bowl revealed that, during hand actuation of the float, the pontoons of the float contacted the interior walls of the test bowl. Further disassembly of the carburetor revealed that the float hinge was worn 0.002 inches beyond its specified limits.

Review of the maintenance records revealed that a “zero time” carburetor was installed when the overhauled engine was installed into the airplane on April 26, 1981. On September 12, 1996, the carburetor fuel bowl gasket was replaced. No other maintenance record entries regarding the carburetor were provided by the airplane owner.

Service Bulletin MSA-3, issued by the carburetor manufacturer and revised on November 18, 1991, included a time between overhaul (TBO) that was the same as the TBO specified by the engine manufacturer for the engine on which the carburetor was installed or 10 years since placed in service or last overhauled, whichever occurs first. 

For Part 91 operators, the carburetor is considered an on-condition item, with no set overhaul period based on calendar or operational time. 

The checklist for Engine Power Loss During Takeoff in the Pilot’s Operating Manual states, “If sufficient runway remains for a normal landing, land straight ahead.” The manual does not specify in that instance to reduce throttle to idle to prevent power application at an inopportune time.

20240916195126.an:
The pilot of the helicopter was performing external lift operations when he noticed an “intermittent and unusual vibration.” The pilot performed a precautionary landing, and a postflight inspection of the main rotor system revealed a crack in one main rotor blade, which constituted substantial damage to the helicopter. 
Postaccident examination of the main rotor blade revealed that a large crack extended from the leading edge spar on the lower surface to the middle of the main rotor blade along the doubler leading edge on the upper surface of the blade. There was an area of chipped paint adjacent to the crack at the outboard tip of the root fitting on the lower side of the blade. After sectioning, the large crack was mechanically exposed and examined stereoscopically. Feathery features consistent with fatigue were observed on the lower side fracture surfaces of the doubler, skin, and spar.
Scanning electron microscope examination revealed numerous ratchet marks at the doubler-skin and skin-spar interfaces emanating at the outboard sides of both layers, consistent with multiple initiation fatigue starting from the outboard side. Dark-colored deposits were observed on the spar fracture surface at the tip and on the adjacent skin fracture surface due to the rubbing of mating fracture surfaces. The large size of the crack and the rubbing of the mating fracture surfaces was consistent with fatigue crack growth over an extended period of time.
The accident helicopter main rotor blades were subject to an FAA Airworthiness Directive (AD) for regular inspections due to the helicopter’s use for external lift operations. The cracked main rotor blade was installed onto the accident helicopter the month before the accident and had accrued about 67 hours of operation since installation. The operator reported that an inspection in accordance with the AD (AD 2005-21-02) was most recently performed 6 days (12.4 flight hours) before the accident. Maintenance personnel noted no defects during recent inspections. 
According to the operator, the inboard portion of the main rotor blade was painted gloss white by the operator’s director of maintenance sometime during the month of the accident; however, there were no maintenance records reflecting when or by whom the painting was performed or inspected. 
It is likely that the fatigue crack occurred sometime between when the main rotor blade was installed onto the helicopter and before the accident flight; however, when the fatigue crack occurred could not be determined. Manufacturer guidance stated that the identification of cracks in main rotor blades requires a careful examination, including the use of supplemental lighting and optical magnification. Whether maintenance personnel performed the inspections with adequate lighting and magnification was not determined. Additionally, it could not be determined whether the fatigue cracking may have been concealed by the recent painting of the main rotor blade.
20240916195126.fa:
On September 11, 2024, about 1400 eastern daylight time, a Hughes 369D helicopter, N8969F, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Canton, Michigan. The pilot was uninjured. The helicopter was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 133 rotorcraft external load flight.
The operator used the helicopter for external lift operations. The purpose of the low-level flight was to support powerline maintenance work. The helicopter was operating from an off-airport landing zone delivering cargo to a powerline structure about 300 yards away.
While in flight, the pilot, who was sitting in the left seat, noticed an “intermittent and unusual vibration.” The pilot performed a precautionary landing and shut down the helicopter without further incident. The pilot performed a visual inspection of the main rotor system, and he observed a crack in the yellow main rotor blade (main rotor blades are typically marked with various colors to easily identify and reference each individual blade). The helicopter sustained substantial damage to the yellow main rotor blade. There was no further damage to the helicopter.
The main rotor blade was manufactured by MD Helicopters (part number 369D21100-523 and serial number 009999-K364) and was subject to a finite life limit of 4,000 total hours. The blade was installed on the helicopter on August 3, 2024, at 3,222.2 total hours. At the time of the accident, the main rotor blade had accumulated 3,289.9 total hours, 67.7 hours since installation, and 6 days (12.4 hours) since the most recent inspection. 
Postaccident examination of the main rotor blade revealed that a large crack extended from the leading edge spar on the lower surface to the middle of the main rotor blade along the doubler leading edge on the upper surface. There was an area of chipped paint adjacent to the crack at the outboard tip of the root fitting on the lower side of the main rotor blade. After sectioning, the large crack in the main rotor blade was mechanically exposed and examined stereoscopically. Feathery features were observed on the lower side fracture surfaces of the doubler, skin, and spar.
Scanning electron microscope examination revealed numerous ratchet marks at the doubler-skin and skin-spar interfaces emanating at the outboard sides of both layers. Dark-colored deposits were observed on the spar fracture surface at the tip and on the adjacent skin fracture surface.
On February 4, 2004, MD Helicopters released Service Bulletin (SB) 369D-201R2, Main Rotor Blade Assembly Torque Event Inspection, which they classified as mandatory compliance. The SB stated that some operators had experienced cracking of the main rotor blades, and that the cracked blades were associated with a high number of torque events (TE), or external lifts per hour. The SB provided procedures for operators to determine the number of TEs accumulated on each main rotor blade in order to establish inspection intervals. The contents of this SB were later adopted into FAA Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2005-21-02 on November 1, 2005, in which the FAA required compliance with the service bulletin and recurring inspections of the main rotor blades at intervals not to exceed 200 TEs or 35 hours time in service, whichever occurs first. MD Helicopters CSP-HMI-2, Handbook of Maintenance Instructions – Servicing and Maintenance, which is applicable to the 369 series, defines TE as “the transition to a hover from forward flight” or “any external lift operation.” The accident main rotor blade part number was subject to this AD. 
The inspection procedures listed for maintenance personnel in AD 2005-21-02 specifically describe the inspection for chordwise cracks protruding from the underside of the root fitting and the doubler (the location and type of cracking found on the accident main rotor blade). The inspection procedures also specify using a bright light and a 10x magnification glass for the inspection of the lower side of the main rotor blades. 
MD Helicopters CSP-HMI-2, Handbook of Maintenance Instructions – Servicing and Maintenance, contains additional guidance for maintenance personnel performing a visual inspection. During a TE inspection, the main rotor blade should be lifted off of the droop stop from the outboard end of the blade. The handbook stated that the bottom side of main rotor blades are more susceptible to cracks. The guidance also contains a caution for TE inspections and states in part that, “A crack can be difficult to find if a bright light is not used.”
According to the operator, the inboard portion of the main rotor blade was painted gloss white by the operator’s director of maintenance sometime in September 2024; however, there were no maintenance records available showing the paint work that was performed, when the paintwork was exactly performed, who performed the paint work, and who inspected the paint work. Instructions contained in MD Helicopters CSP-HMI-2 stated: 
It is recommended to only paint the inboard 24 inch (60.96 cm) gloss white to help with crack detection. All blades must be painted the same.
The operator’s maintenance records revealed that a TE inspection in compliance with FAA AD 2005-21-02 was most recently performed on September 5, 2024, at a helicopter total time of 18,306.4 hours and TE of 83,119. Since the main rotor blade was installed, four compliance entries with FAA AD 2005-21-02 were found in the operator’s maintenance records, with three different company mechanics performing that work. All four compliance entries contained a note stating, “no defects.”
The MD Helicopters MD 500D (Model 369D) Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) discusses preflight inspection procedures and states, in part, for the pilot to check:
Main rotor blades for chordwise cracks on the underside of the blade skin and doubler. If existing, the cracks will be at the leading and trailing edges of the root fitting in the area of the two most outboard bolts or outermost end of the lower root fitting.
The RFM does not require the use of supplemental lighting, such as a flashlight, during the preflight inspection.
The RFM contains an emergency procedure for abnormal vibrations and lists the indications as, “sudden, unusual, or excessive vibrations occurring during flight.” The manual states that the onset of unusual or excessive vibrations in the helicopter may be an indication of problems in the rotor drive or drive train systems, and that the pilot should land as soon as possible to have the cause of vibration identified and corrected before any further flights.
On October 2, 2024, MD Helicopters released Service Letter (SL) 369D-144, Inspection of the Main Rotor Blades Assemblies. The SL recommends that owners and operators ensure that inspections per MD Helicopters Service Bulletin 369D-201R2 are completed and FAA AD 2005-21-02 are referenced. The document further states in part:
Failure to comply with the bulletin can cause the loss of a main rotor blade during operation and cause significant vibrations and a loss of helicopter control.

20240917195131.an: The pilot reported that he launched his hot air balloon for a brief solo flight with the intent of practicing maneuvers during calm wind conditions. Shortly after departure, he prepared for landing on a spot about 1/4-mile away that consisted of a flat harvested corn field. During the landing approach, he observed a powerline perpendicular to his final approach and landing target. He initially thought about climbing, but realized the balloon would not react fast enough, so he opened the vent to deflate the envelope and descend. The balloon envelope did not vent quickly enough and the balloon drifted into the powerlines, resulting in electrical arcing until the electrical breaker shut off. The basket settled onto the ground and the balloon envelope remained partially inflated and draped over the powerlines. The arcing resulted in substantial damage to the balloon; 6 cables were severed and there were multiple burn holes in the envelope. The pilot reported that there were no pre impact mechanical malfunctions or failures of the balloon that would have precluded normal operation or performance.
